headline: Iteration-level batching does not guarantee throughput capacity under latency SLOs at high load.
claim: Iteration-level batching can improve throughput by avoiding request-level padding, but it does not guarantee higher serving capacity under latency SLOs when prefill interference dominates at high load.
paper_fact: The interleaving of prefills and decodes involves a trade-off between throughput and latency for current LLM inference schedulers.
premise: Serving capacity is maximum QPS under a latency target, not raw tokens per second; prefill interference can make TBT the binding constraint.
inference: At high load, eager prefill admission can cause generation stalls that cap capacity under a TBT SLO, so the throughput benefit of iteration-level batching is conditional on admission policy and load.
toy_example: Toy example (not a measurement): a long prefill admitted eagerly delays decodes; if the TBT SLO is tight, the system cannot sustain the higher QPS even though batch membership is dynamic.
conditional_consequence: If load is high and prefill admission is eager, TBT SLO may cap capacity; if prefill tokens are chunked or throttled, capacity can improve.
critical_link: Capacity is measured under an SLO, and the mechanism does not control prefill interference or per-iteration prefill token count.
defeaters: No latency SLO
Decode-only workload
Disaggregated prefill and decode
Short prompts
Low load
do_not_infer: Do not infer iteration-level batching always improves capacity
Do not infer raw throughput equals serving capacity
Do not infer high load always erases the benefit
author_boundaries: Paper reports that vLLM and Orca trade TBT latency for high throughput
Paper does not claim iteration-level batching alone maximizes capacity under all SLOs

State-of-the-art systems today use prefill-prioritizing schedules that trade TBT latency for high throughput.

evidence.support_description: The interleaving of prefills and decodes involves a trade-off between throughput and latency for current LLM inference schedulers.

mechanism: Serving capacity is maximum QPS under a latency target, not raw tokens per second; prefill interference can make TBT the binding constraint. At high load, eager prefill admission can cause generation stalls that cap capacity under a TBT SLO, so the throughput benefit of iteration-level batching is conditional on admission policy and load.

headline: Reducing pipeline bubbles does not guarantee lower TBT latency.
claim: Bubble reduction is primarily a throughput/capacity effect; it does not by itself guarantee lower time-between-tokens or time-to-first-token, because chunked prefills and token-budget choices can trade latency.
paper_fact: Sarathi-Serve also reduces pipeline bubbles, resulting in up to 5.6× gains in end-to-end serving capacity for Falcon-180B deployed with pipeline parallelism.
premise: Throughput and latency are distinct objectives; a schedule can improve one while worsening another.
inference: Bubble reduction can raise capacity without guaranteeing per-request latency; latency depends on token budget and chunking.
toy_example: Toy example (not a measurement): a schedule with zero bubbles but a very small token budget may still have high TTFT due to chunk overhead.
conditional_consequence: If SLO is strict, smaller token budget may be needed, reducing efficiency; if relaxed, larger budget may improve throughput but increase TBT variation.
critical_link: The paper measures capacity under SLOs and separately reports TTFT/TBT effects of components; bubble reduction is tied to capacity gains, not directly to TBT.
defeaters: bubble reduction also reduces queueing delay enough to improve TBT indirectly
paper shows Sarathi-Serve lowers TBT in Table 4 when combined
workload is throughput-only with no latency SLO
do_not_infer: do not infer bubble reduction always lowers TBT

headline: Tile-quantization-aware chunk sizing does not imply or guarantee an optimal token budget for throughput-latency tradeoff.
claim: The paper's tile-quantization effect is one factor in token-budget selection; optimizing for tile alignment can conflict with TBT SLO and pipeline-bubble minimization, so an aligned chunk is not the same as the serving goal.
paper_fact: Larger chunks lead to higher inter-batch runtime variations that result in pipeline bubbles which results in lower overall system throughput. On the other hand, picking a very small token budget can lead to higher overhead due to lower arithmetic intensity and other fixed overheads.
premise: Token budget controls both prefill efficiency and decode latency; larger chunks improve prefill efficiency but can increase TBT and pipeline bubbles, while smaller chunks reduce latency but add chunking overhead.
inference: Tile alignment is a local stopping criterion, not the global objective; the token budget must be chosen by trading off TBT SLO, chunking overhead, pipeline bubbles, and hardware tile effects.
toy_example: Not a measurement: an aligned 2048-token chunk may improve prefill efficiency but increase TBT under a strict SLO; illustrative only.
conditional_consequence: If alignment favors a larger chunk under a strict TBT SLO, the aligned choice may violate latency; if it favors a very small chunk, chunking overhead may reduce throughput.
critical_link: Alignment must be evaluated inside a token-budget search that satisfies the TBT SLO and pipeline-parallelism constraints, not as a standalone objective.

pipeline-bubble effects considered when using PP

headline: Maximizing capacity under a TBT SLO does not imply or guarantee meeting TTFT or end-to-end cost goals.
claim: Token-budget selection is framed around TBT SLO and chunking overhead to maximize capacity; it does not by itself guarantee TTFT or overall cost objectives, which are separate latency and utilization concerns.
paper_fact: The token budget is determined based on two competing factors — TBT SLO requirement and chunked-prefills overhead.
premise: TBT and TTFT are distinct metrics; a policy that maximizes QPS under a TBT constraint can still queue requests and affect TTFT or cost.
inference: A budget that is optimal for capacity under P99 TBT may not be optimal for applications with strict TTFT or cost targets.
toy_example: Toy example, not a measurement: a workload with strict 200 ms TTFT but relaxed 1 s TBT could accept a large token budget that meets TBT yet queues requests beyond TTFT.
conditional_consequence: If the application objective includes TTFT or cost rather than only TBT-constrained capacity, the selected token budget may need to be different.
critical_link: The critical link is objective mismatch: the stopping rule is TBT-feasible capacity, while the goal may include TTFT and cost.

headline: Balanced arithmetic intensity does not imply or guarantee meeting the TBT SLO
claim: Sarathi-Serve's balanced hybrid batches maximize compute and bandwidth utilization, but arithmetic-intensity balance is only a utilization proxy and does not by itself guarantee the P99 TBT SLO.
paper_fact: Sarathi-Serve forms balanced batches by combining decodes and prefill chunks to maximize both compute and bandwidth utilization.
premise: Arithmetic intensity and utilization are hardware/operator-level metrics; TBT SLO is an end-to-end tail-latency requirement. A batch can be balanced yet still exceed a latency bound if its absolute work is too large or if tail effects dominate.
inference: The mechanism's balance property is not a latency guarantee; it must be paired with token-budget selection and SLO validation.
conditional_consequence: If the token budget is chosen so each hybrid iteration's compute fits the TBT budget, balance can help utilization; if not, balanced batches can still violate P99 TBT.
critical_link: The missing link is a per-iteration latency bound: arithmetic-intensity balance does not bound absolute iteration time or tail latency.
necessary_conditions: Token budget calibrated to TBT SLO
defeaters: Measured P99 TBT under SLO across token budgets
Dynamic token budget
Workloads where balance directly bounds iteration time
do_not_infer: Balanced batches always meet SLO
High utilization equals low tail latency
Token budget is workload-independent

headline: Prefill-prioritizing eager admission conflicts with high capacity under strict TBT SLO at high load or long prompts
claim: At high load or with long prompts under a strict TBT SLO, generation stalls can dominate and cap capacity despite the throughput proxy of larger decode batches.
paper_fact: The maximum capacity of vLLM gets capped due to generation stalls under stringent TBT SLOs.
premise: At high load, queueing and long prefill durations make latency SLOs bind before throughput saturates.
inference: The throughput proxy can be dominated by generation stalls, so capacity under strict SLO can be lower than a stall-free schedule.
toy_example: Toy example (not a measurement): at high load, a queue of long prompts can keep admitting whole prefills and delay decodes; this illustrates the mechanism, not a measured result.
conditional_consequence: If load is high and prompts are long under strict SLO, capacity is capped; if load is low or SLO is relaxed, eager admission may still help.
critical_link: Load and prompt-length distribution relative to SLO slack.
defeaters: chunked prefills
disaggregation

headline: Decode-prioritizing request-level batching does not imply efficient GPU utilization or low TTFT
claim: Optimizing TBT by admitting new requests only when no decodes remain does not guarantee efficient GPU utilization, high serving capacity, or low time-to-first-token for queued requests.
paper_fact: "This approach reduces the operational complexity of the scheduling framework but at the expense of inefficient resource utilization."
premise: TTFT includes queueing and admission delay; GPU utilization depends on batch size and padding; TBT is only inter-token latency.
inference: Decode-prioritizing can leave GPU compute idle and delay new requests, so TBT optimization is not a proxy for TTFT or utilization.
toy_example: Toy example (not a measurement): many requests arrive while a long batch decodes; they wait until the batch completes, so TTFT grows even if admitted decodes have stable TBT.
conditional_consequence: If many requests queue while a long batch decodes, TTFT increases; if batch sizes are small, utilization drops. If load is low, these costs may be small.
critical_link: Admission only when no decodes remain delays new prefills and can leave decode-only iterations with small batch sizes.
necessary_conditions: TTFT or utilization is a relevant objective
defeaters: low load
short batches
iteration-level batching
disaggregated prefill/decode

Do not infer that TBT is poor under this mechanism.

headline: A capacity metric defined by a P99 TBT SLO does not imply or guarantee application-level latency quality or rankings when TTFT or mean latency is the primary objective
claim: M10's capacity metric, defined by P99 TBT SLO and a median scheduling-delay limit, does not guarantee application-level latency quality or rankings when TTFT or mean latency is the primary objective.
paper_fact: We focus on the median value for the TTFT since this metric is obtained only once per user request and on the 99th percentile (P99) for TBT values since every decode token results in a TBT latency value.
premise: Applications differ in which latency percentile and metric they optimize; a system can meet a P99 TBT SLO while having poor median TTFT or mean latency.
inference: Therefore, capacity numbers and rankings from M10 are conditional on the chosen SLO and metric and should not be read as general serving-quality guarantees.
toy_example: Toy example (not a measurement): two systems A and B have equal capacity under a P99 TBT SLO, but A has much worse median TTFT; an application gated on TTFT would not treat them as equal.
conditional_consequence: If an application's primary latency objective is TTFT or mean latency rather than P99 TBT, then M10 capacity rankings may not match that application's goals.
critical_link: The link is the metric definition: capacity is max QPS subject to P99 TBT and median scheduling delay, not subject to TTFT or mean latency.

claim: M10's sustainability check uses a 2-second median scheduling-delay limit; passing it does not guarantee that tail queueing delay or tail TTFT is acceptable.

conditional_consequence: If an application has a tail TTFT or tail queueing requirement, M10 capacity may overstate acceptable load.

headline: SLO multiples tied to decode-iteration time do not imply or guarantee relevance to other application SLOs
claim: M10's strict and relaxed SLOs are defined as 5x and 25x a model-hardware-specific decode-iteration time; capacity rankings under these SLOs do not guarantee rankings under different absolute or relative SLOs.
paper_fact: we define the SLO on P99 TBT to be equal to 5× and 25× the execution time of a decode iteration for a request (with prefill length of 4k and 32 batch size) running without any prefill interference for the strict and relaxed settings, respectively.
premise: Application SLOs are not generally proportional to a particular model-hardware decode-iteration time; changing the SLO threshold can change which system has higher capacity.
inference: Thus M10's capacity rankings are conditional on its SLO construction and do not guarantee rankings under other SLOs.
toy_example: Toy example (not a measurement): an application with a 300 ms P99 TBT SLO could rank two systems differently from the 5x/25x decode-iteration SLOs.
conditional_consequence: If an application's P99 TBT SLO differs materially from the 5x/25x definitions, the reported capacity advantage may change.
critical_link: The SLO baseline is computed from a decode iteration with prefill length 4k and batch size 32 without prefill interference, coupling the threshold to model, hardware, and workload assumptions.
